page: Amazon Web Services m3.xlarge is an earlier-generation general-purpose virtual machine executed via the Xen hypervisor. It is powered by a dedicated 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor on the x86_64 architecture. The hardware allocation delivers 4 vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores using hyper-threading, supported by 25 MB of L3 cache. Memory capacity is provisioned at 15.0 GB, yielding 3.75 GB of RAM per vCPU. Storage is bundled directly with an integrated 80 GB local SSD, and baseline network throughput is rated at 1 Gbps. No GPU accelerators are present on this instance type.

Performance benchmarks reflect the vintage of the underlying Ivy Bridge hardware. Computational metrics generally place the instance in the lower percentiles across synthetic tests. Single-core and multi-core Stress-ng evaluations score 1268.59 and 3349.67 respectively, while Geekbench scores record 702.0 for single-core and 1505.0 for multi-core execution. The PassMark memory test achieves an average category rating at 1944.74, but database operations register lower at 1376.56, and Redis SET throughput caps at 1.46 million operations per second. Hardware instruction support includes AVX and AES, but lacks newer extensions such as AVX2, AVX-512, or AMX.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m3.xlarge exhibits diminished compute throughput per resource unit relative to modern server generations. The primary structural advantage remains its included 80 GB local SSD storage paired with a standard general-purpose memory ratio. Consequently, this server type is best suited for legacy application hosting, non-critical staging or development environments, basic internal tools, and low-concurrency web serving that relies on ephemeral local storage rather than high CPU throughput.
description: Amazon Web Services m3.xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the Xen hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. It provides 4 dedicated vCPUs from a 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 dual-core processor with hyper-threading, accompanied by 15.0 GB of memory and a bundled 80 GB local SSD. Network bandwidth is provisioned at a 1 Gbps baseline, and the instance includes no GPU acceleration. Benchmark measurements show lower-tier performance in modern terms, with Geekbench recording 702.0 in single-core and 1505.0 in multi-core tests, alongside a Stress-ng multi-core score of 3349.67 and an average PassMark memory score of 1944.74. While modern architectures surpass its computational density, the bundled local disk and balanced memory profile make the instance functional for legacy workloads, development environments, and low-traffic web serving.
